 ‼️ Wie die USA auf den Ausfall von Systemen reagieren ‼️ 
 
In der letzten Woche traf es die USA Schlag auf Schlag.
 👉 Zuerst Ausfall von Microsoft – der Fehler störte System 24 Stunden.
 👉 Am 13. November (Freitag) dann die der FAA Kommunikationssysteme, welches Starts in ganz USA erst mal für Stunden aussetzte.
 👉 Dann traf es  am 15. die Amazon Web Services.
 👉 Am 16. die  JPMorgan Chase, mit Auswirkungen bei Wells Fargo, Bank of America und Zelle.
 👉 Nicht genug, am gleichen Tag gab es bei der Airline United einen Systemausfall.
 👉 Auch Apple wurde nicht verschont – am 17. Störungen in der Cloud, App Store, Apple Pay und Apple Music.
 👉 Und zum Schluss am 17.11. noch das sensibelste der USA das NSA Netzwerk.

 ➡️ Einiges war nicht wirklich gut erklärt. Und zuletzt glaubte keiner mehr so richtig, das es kein Hybrider Angriff war.

Letztlich: 
 ❗ Die Bevölkerung ist in den USA irritiert – und als Resulat begannen Hamsterkäufe. ❗ 
 
In den Supermärkten waren Wasserflaschen, Kurbelradios bald Mangelware. Ebenso meldeten einige Baumärkte den Ausverkauf von tragbaren Generatoren.
 
Geschürt wurden die Gerüchte auch noch von diversen Republikanern:
 👉 „Die Amerikaner sehen alles, was bei diesen Serviceausfällen passiert, und haben das Gefühl, nicht die ganze Wahrheit zu erfahren Senator Josh Hawley, Republikaner aus Missouri,
 
 👉 „Wenn das alles Zufall ist, dann ist es der größte Zufall in der Geschichte der Welt“, schrieb Senator Rick Scott Republikaner aus Florida.

Man beschwichtigte – aber die Prepper hatten ihre beste Zeit. Über X und Facebook wurde sofort verbreitet, was alles benötigt wird. Einige US-Bürger berichteten, das sie Vorräte im Wert von über 3.500 USD besorgt haben, inkl. Propangasflaschen für eine mobile Heizung.

PS 06:30h: Es hat wohl jetzt auch Spuren im W.H. hinterlassen:
 ➡️ Oberster Cyberexperte im Weißen Haus tritt nach diversen IT-Ausfällen ab
Er dürfte eine eher arbeitsreiche Woche hinter sich haben – nun braucht er einen neuen Job: Mitten im Chaos um Nvidia und IT-Probleme bei Großkonzernen verlässt Cyber-Direktor Sean Cairncross das Weiße Haus.

If an AI agent you authorized gets hacked and drains your account, five of America's biggest banks now say the loss is yours.

TechCrunch reported this week that Citi updated its terms: customers who give a third-party AI agent access to their accounts are responsible for what happens through it, including when the tool leaks credentials or gets hacked. PNC changed its terms on Wednesday, Citizens emailed customers with the same message, and JPMorgan and Bank of America made similar moves last month. One telling detail: Citi's own AI agents are exempt.

Motives are mixed, as they were with United last week. The security risk is real. Reportedly, banks also worry that AI tools could help customers dodge fees and chase better rates, which cuts into revenue. Both can be true at once.

Put it next to the other stories this month and a pattern appears. United blocks unauthorized agents. OpenAI's new wallet keeps your card number from its agents and puts your approval on your device. Banks say don't hand over your password. The direction is clear: agents are welcome through approved, scoped channels, and handing over your credentials is on you.

Practical takeaways: don't give an AI tool your banking password, prefer official integrations that use limited-access tokens, and read your bank's agreement. Terms vary, and they're written subject to applicable law, so I'm not claiming what a court would enforce. This isn't legal advice.

Who should carry the loss when an AI agent you authorized gets hacked: you, your bank, or the agent's maker?

I connected my Bank of America card to Claude through Plaid. Here’s what changed: I no longer have to open my banking app every time I want to check my latest charges or see where my money went this week. I just ask. And if I need to buy something, an agent can do it for me if it has a way to pay and I’ve authorized the purchase.

I now have three agents on my desktop: Duet running on Anthropic’s Claude, Muse from Meta, and Dots in OpenAI’s ChatGPT. I call my Dot Bax, and my Muse goes by Jarvis.

So I basically have three personal assistants now. They book hotels, reply to emails, schedule meetings, go through Telegram conversations, pull together stats, and write reports. At the end of the week, they might even suggest booking a table at a bar and grabbing a beer :)

I’ve given them context on my projects and shown them how I like to work. If something urgent comes up during a call, I can ask them to put together a quick briefing on the spot.

But back to Plaid and open banking APIs. My understanding is that Kazakhstan is developing this infrastructure too. Once AI agents become part of everyday life, the banking app will stop being the first place customers go. And banks will have to compete on terms again. An agent can compare the total cost, check the cashback restrictions, and spot what’s buried in the fine print.

It might say, “You’ll get a better deal on this purchase if you don’t use Kaspi. And this month, have your salary paid into your Bank RBK account: based on how you spend, you’ll earn more cashback.” Kaspi and RBK are just examples.

So if you’re building a super app, I’d also ask: how can you make your products and services available to AI agents, say through ChatGPT Business? And how can you offer terms that actually win when compared side by side? No clutter. No hidden fees buried in the fine print.

¿Cómo están cuidando los bancos tu cuenta frente a los asistentes de IA?

Un agente de IA es un asistente que no solo responde, también actúa por ti, por ejemplo entrando a tu cuenta o moviendo dinero. Es una herramienta nueva, y los bancos están definiendo cómo convivir con ella.

Según el Financial Times, Citigroup y Bank of America están poniendo límites a ese acceso, y antes lo hicieron JPMorgan Chase y Charles Schwab. Lo hacen mientras las reglas y las responsabilidades se terminan de definir.

Según los reportes, Citi indica que busca proteger las cuentas y la información de sus clientes. Pide no compartir las claves con estas herramientas, y lo que haga el agente se trata como hecho por el cliente. Bank of America mantiene el límite mientras define quién responde por los pagos que autorice una IA, y considera que una persona debería aprobar cada salida de dinero.

El informe también señala que los bancos vigilan el riesgo de que los agentes muevan el efectivo inactivo hacia inversiones con mayor rendimiento.

Hoy esas reglas siguen en definición y cambian de un banco a otro.

#InteligenciaArtificial #Banca #AgentesDeIA

Citi actualizó su acuerdo de usuario en línea: quien le da acceso a su cuenta a un agente de IA de terceros responde por lo que haga ese agente. Según TechCrunch, eso incluye lo que hagan atacantes si la herramienta filtra las credenciales o la hackean. PNC cambió sus términos el 18 de noviembre, Citizens avisó a sus clientes por correo, y JPMorgan y Bank of America anunciaron políticas parecidas en octubre. El contrato de PNC prohíbe dar contraseñas o códigos a un agente y, en general, no permite que inicie pagos sin autorización del banco. Son bancos de EE. UU. y sus términos están sujetos a la ley aplicable. Aun así, la pregunta de quién paga cuando un agente se equivoca llegará a cualquier negocio que automatice pagos. Antes de darle acceso a un agente de IA, lee el contrato, define límites y revisa los movimientos.

Hyderabad has secured another landmark global investment in its commercial real estate sector, with US-based financial services giant Bank of America leasing over 10 lakh sq. ft. of office space at Mindspace Cyberabad in Madhapur for its Global Capability Centre (GCC).

The 12-year lease agreement, signed through its Indian subsidiary BA Continuum India, carries an estimated rental commitment of nearly ₹1,500 crore, making it one of India's largest individual office leasing transactions of 2026.

- Initial rental rate of ₹82 per sq. ft. per month.

AI News Today (Nov 20, 2026): Record IPO Day After, Banks Shift AI-Agent Risk, and Security Teams Get Agent Tools
Here are the AI stories I'm tracking as the week closes.
1. The record IPO sets the tone
Anthropic's shares rose on their first day of trading on Nasdaq after the company priced at $83 and raised a record $81.3B, according to NPR. CEO Dario Amodei said the company will prioritize safety and human control over business or political pressure, and that its stronger financial position supports that commitment. The market will now watch how public investors value frontier AI labs, and what it means for any future listings.

2. Banks are shifting AI-agent risk to customers
Citi, PNC and Citizens updated their terms on November 18 to hold customers responsible for anything third-party AI agents do in their accounts, including after credentials leak or an agent is hacked. JPMorgan and Bank of America reportedly moved first.
Takeaway: if your product lets an agent act for a user, expect legal terms, permissions and audit logs to become part of the design.

3. Safety testing is under the spotlight
The US GAO reportedly found that ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok each produced viable attack plans in under 12 hours when tested. It is a reminder that safeguards need continuous, independent testing.

4. Security teams get agent tooling
At Microsoft Ignite 2026, Microsoft launched Perception, which lets security teams coordinate AI agents through automated playbooks. EY and Microsoft also opened an agentic cyber defence centre, and ADNOC is layering OpenAI's agent platform on its own AI.

• The New York Times reports Alibaba used Megaspeed GPU capacity to aid a Chinese military-linked AI lab, while The Information reports a senior Commerce official pressed staff to fast-track Nvidia H200 exports to China.

6. Robotics and autonomy
MegaRobo raised about $200M for AI-powered lab and factory robotics, and Gatik raised $200M to scale autonomous freight.

My takeaway as a full stack developer: this week showed AI maturing into regulated, insured, audited infrastructure. The developers who can combine AI features with security, permissions and compliance will have the edge.

Who pays when an AI agent goes wrong? More US banks say you do

According to TechCrunch, Citi, PNC and Citizens updated their terms on November 18 to hold customers responsible for anything third-party AI agents do in their accounts. That includes activity after credentials are leaked or the agent itself is hacked. JPMorgan and Bank of America adopted similar terms last month.

Meanwhile, agents keep arriving in everyday products. A job posting suggests Apple is building a proactive agentic assistant that coordinates sub-agents, and Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman says it could ship as early as 2027.

Why this matters:
 → Liability is being settled in the fine print. If you connect an agent to your bank account, the new terms put the risk on you, including when the agent is hacked.
 → Five major banks now follow the same pattern. That makes it a trend across US banking, not one bank’s policy.
 → Agents are heading into more products anyway. As assistants start acting on your behalf, expect more of the same question: who is responsible when they act?

👇 Would you connect an AI agent to your bank account if you were liable for everything it does?

One of my favorite weeks of the year is also one of the Wichita Symphony’s biggest operations: Young People’s Concerts. This week, we welcomed students from 17 Kansas school districts, along with private schools and homeschool groups, giving thousands of kids the chance to experience a live symphony orchestra.

These performances were especially exciting because, instead of bringing in a packaged show, the concert was conceived and written right here at the Wichita Symphony by our own Matt Blauer. Matt plays trombone in the orchestra and also serves as our Artistic Personnel & Community Engagement Manager.

An event at this scale really is an all-hands effort. Our small staff takes on different roles for the day, and we simply couldn’t do it without a small army of volunteers. 🇮🇩 Indonésie : la banque centrale devrait jouer la prudence le 18 novembre

Bank Indonesia réunit son conseil des gouverneurs les 17 et 18 novembre. Selon les économistes de Bank of America, elle devrait maintenir son taux directeur à 5,75 %.

📊 Les indicateurs lui donnent raison :

Inflation : 3,23 % sur un an en octobre, dans la cible de la banque centrale
Déficit courant : prévu à 1,8 % du PIB en 2026, en hausse mais maîtrisé

🇹🇭 L’écart avec la Thaïlande reste frappant : pour défendre la roupie, l’Indonésie a relevé son taux de 4,75 % à 5,75 % cette année, tandis que la Banque de Thaïlande le maintient à 1 %.

⚠️ Deux risques pourraient changer la donne :

Une hausse des prix des carburants subventionnés
Une nouvelle poussée de volatilité de la roupie, alors que MSCI envisage toujours de retirer l’Indonésie de la catégorie des marchés émergents
